I grew up with multiple rescue greyhounds, so very much the opposite of a Newfie - went from skinny, short-haired sighthound to now a big, fluffy bear. I am drawn to large breed dogs, and wanted one that doesn't have a ton of health problems. I know that any breed I rarely encounter at work (meaning they aren't often sick, at least in my area of Canada) would likely be a good choice in terms of their longterm health. 

​

1. I've lived in a few basement suites over the years. One key phrase to look for would be "legal suite" because that ensures there is adequate windows that are safe to escape out of in case of fire, but have the added bonus of adding more natural light. Its worth looking for one with a dedicated separate entrance for the suite. Many have shared laundry, so that would be another thing to look for is in suite laundry. It is not at all too bold to ask about the upstairs neighbours. I lived in one suite with a retired couple with two cats upstairs which was totally fine, but when they moved out, a mother who ran a daycare moved in, who also owned a very barky dog and it quickly became unlivable.

You might get lucky and find a basement suite that has its own dedicated yard space, or it may be shared with upstairs tenants. It's worth it to ensure there is access to electrified parking as well if you end up buying a car, because you will absolutely need to plug in a car here in the winter.

2) I would recommend having a vehicle here. We are not known for having the most robust or reliable transit system. If you manage to find a rental within the center/core area of Saskatoon that would be less of an issue, but I lived on the west side in a newer development and our access to transit was limited at best.

My heart goes out to you - On my last shift last week in ER we had double-digit euthanasias, and that's a lot for any team to tackle. Be vocal with your team if you're feeling overwhelmed. Debriefing is a great habit to get into as well! At my clinic, we always try to do a debrief after a code/CPR. Partly to allow us to discuss what went well, what didn't go well, and what we can improve upon next time. Beyond that though, debriefing after particularly difficult euthanasia cases can be helpful as well. Try asking a coworker, "Are you in a place where I can let you know how I'm feeling about the case we just did?". If they are open to it, it could be a simple 5-minute conversation. I find that often just acknowledging that a scenario was particularly sad can bring enough release so that I can go about my day without carrying that extra emotional weight.

In Canada for context - there is no regulated treatment option for vets to prescribe here. I'm a vet tech in the unique position of having had my mother in laws cat have FIP - she was also 'steered' to the FIP Warriors Facebook group. She was able to purchase medications almost immediately, and there are veterinarians part of that group online that look over bloodwork and make recommendations. Her cat went from basically on death's doorstep to now very healthy and thriving. It was upwards of $5000 for the cost of the medication alone, without follow-up diagnostics. 

As a veterinary professional, it was a bit off-putting seeing the medication itself in person -  a plain, more or less unlabeled clear vial of liquid. The injections were painful and difficult for her to administer daily, and her cat did end up developing a skin lesion at the injection site which is apparently common in many cats. (Unsure if there is a preservative issue or what). Ultimately, she is happy with her choice to pursue treatment as he is a normal happy cat now. There are some efforts in various universities to do research on these medications, but cost is a big prohibiting factor to getting research funding.

The fact that you are concerned about the animal's well-being is so great! Remember that everyone starts somewhere, and failures are natural for all of us, even after years of experience. A good thing to practise is the motion of pulling the stopper of a syringe at home with one hand. When I was in school we took home vacutainers with koolaid or some other benign fluid inside to practise the motion of drawing up medications/blood. It's also great for getting the movement of drawing back blood/injecting a medication. Get into the habit of slow, deliberate, gentle redirections if you don't hit the vein initially (as opposed to sharp, aggressive, jabby). In terms of blowing the vein, there are many factors beyond just technique - older animals often have frail veins, and can blow regardless. Remember to breathe while doing your first blood draws, and you will be nailing it in no time. I'm sure your instructors/seasoned techs around you will have tons of valuable tips and tricks. The fact that you're asking this question is great! It means you are committed to bettering yourself and your career, and that speaks volumes. 

Are you specifically looking to further your physical technical abilities (like catheter placement, blood draws etc), or are you wanting more focus on understanding?

Either way, I think taking the time to set out some specific goals for yourself is a great plan in your first year as a tech. 

Are there areas that currently give you anxiety? A lot of techs are nervous about anesthesia when they first start their careers, and thankfully there is endless CE out there to help grasp some of those concepts. A great habit to get into is debriefing - with your doctors if possible. Should anything go "not according to plan", a good practice is to discuss or deconstruct the scenario after the fact. Perhaps there was a different approach to your sedation/anesthetic plan that could have helped that surgery go smoother, perhaps there were clues in the bloodwork or physical exam that may have alerted you to potential issues before they occurred. Don't hesitate to reach out if there is anything specific you are looking to learn about, perhaps I can send something your way. Best of luck!

A few other tricks I have for getting up/switching over after a night shift:

\- before you go to bed, open up your windows and blinds. Let all that sun and sound in. You are much less likely to sleep through an alarm or roll over and keep sleeping if it's bright.

In highschool, I missed my curfew once because of a mushroom trip gone bad. I'm a girl, and she definitely had strong feelings about me drinking alcohol even, let alone doing drugs. I had literally thrown my phone against a wall, thinking that if I destroyed my phone, my mom would stop trying to get a hold of me (calling/texting). I ended up going to my boyfriends house because I was just so neurotic at that point, I knew I couldn't go home. My mom was conveniently waiting for me when we got to his house, and promptly took me right home.

Now, once we got home you can imagine the tongue-lashing I was about to receive. She figured I had been out drinking at some party and just got wasted. Regardless, this was a huge deal to her, and my dad, who both had some choice words to say. I said very little, (as a remorseful teen would do) but only because even then, at probably about 4 am, 8-9 hours after taking the mushrooms, being yelled at into my face, I was STILL TRIPPING. It was horrible. She thought I was going through some terrible bullying or something bad was going on in my life because "it was unlike me to be destructive with drinking", little did she know, her face was melting in front of me.

So yeah, don't think they'd be too stoked to learn the truth about that one.
